questions.question: What are the two ways to create a thread in Java?
questions.title: Two Ways to Create Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: You can create a thread by extending the Thread class and overriding run(), or by implementing the Runnable interface and passing it to a Thread constructor. A third modern approach is implementing Callable for tasks that return a value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of fundamental thread creation mechanisms and when to use each approach in production code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking extending Thread is the preferred approach, when composition via Runnable is better because Java doesn't support multiple inheritance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Immediately state that Runnable is preferred in production because it separates the task from the thread execution mechanism and allows the class to extend other classes.

sections.title: Two Mechanisms for Thread Creation
sections.content:
Java provides two fundamental ways to create threads: **extending Thread** and **implementing Runnable**. Think of Thread as the worker itself, while Runnable is the job description.

When you extend Thread, you're saying "I am a thread that does this specific work." When you implement Runnable, you're saying "Here's a task that any thread can execute." The Runnable approach is preferred in production because it follows the **composition over inheritance** principle — your class can extend another class while still being runnable in a thread. This matters because Java only allows single inheritance, so extending Thread locks you out of extending other useful classes like business domain objects or framework components.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Extend Thread|~Override run()|uses single inheritance|task tied to thread|less flexible
blue|Implement Runnable|~Pass to a Thread|class free to extend|works with executors|preferred
emerald|Shared Idea|~Both define run()|start() spawns thread|run() alone = no thread|you need start()
violet|Recommendation|~Runnable wins|composition over inheritance|reusable tasks|pool-ready

sections.title: Thread vs Runnable Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Extending Thread | Implementing Runnable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inheritance | Cannot extend other classes | Free to extend other classes |
| Reusability | Thread and task tightly coupled | Task can run on any thread |
| Thread pool usage | Not suitable for ExecutorService | Works seamlessly with thread pools |
| Object semantics | Represents a thread of execution | Represents a unit of work |
| Modern practice | Rarely used in production | Standard approach for concurrent tasks |

sections.title: Creating Threads Both Ways
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **Runnable** in almost all production scenarios: when building REST services that handle concurrent requests, when submitting tasks to an ExecutorService thread pool, or when your task class already extends a domain class like BaseService.

Use **extending Thread** only in rare cases where you need to customize thread behavior itself — for example, overriding interrupt() for custom cleanup logic, or building a specialized thread class with specific lifecycle hooks. In a Spring Boot application processing customer orders, you'd implement Runnable for order processing tasks so your OrderProcessor can extend BaseProcessor while remaining executable in the web container's thread pool.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Extending Thread when composition is needed**: Freshers often extend Thread first, then realize they need to extend another class like HttpServlet or BaseService, forcing a complete rewrite. The code compiles but locks you into a design corner.
- **Not understanding the new Thread() requirement**: When using Runnable, freshers forget that you still need to wrap it in a Thread object and call start() — they expect the Runnable to magically start running on its own.
- **Reusing Thread instances**: After a thread completes, freshers try to call start() again on the same Thread object, which throws IllegalThreadStateException. Each Thread instance can only be started once.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Extending Thread**: Creates a class that IS-A thread, limits inheritance, rarely used in production code
- **Implementing Runnable**: Creates a class that HAS-A task, allows extending other classes, preferred approach
- **Composition over inheritance**: Runnable separates the task logic from the thread mechanism, enabling reuse
- **ExecutorService compatibility**: Runnable works seamlessly with thread pools, Thread objects do not
- **Single inheritance limitation**: Java allows only one parent class, so extending Thread blocks other inheritance
- **start() is always required**: Both approaches need new Thread(...).start() to create a new OS thread
- **Modern Java patterns**: Lambdas and method references work with Runnable because it's a functional interface

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are two main ways to create a thread in Java. First, you can extend the Thread class and override the run method with your task logic. Second, you can implement the Runnable interface and pass that to a Thread constructor. The Runnable approach is preferred in production code because it uses composition instead of inheritance. That's important because Java doesn't support multiple inheritance, so if you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class like a business domain object or service base class. When you implement Runnable, your class is free to extend something else while still being executable in a thread. In a real Spring Boot service handling API requests, you'd implement Runnable for background tasks so they can extend framework classes and also work with ExecutorService thread pools. The Thread approach is really only used when you need to customize thread behavior itself, like overriding interrupt handling, which is rare. One common mistake is extending Thread first, then realizing you need to extend another class and having to refactor everything. Always start with Runnable unless you have a specific reason to extend Thread.

questions.question: What happens if you call run() instead of start() on a Thread?
questions.title: run() vs start() on a Thread Object
questions.direct_answer: Calling run() directly executes the code in the current thread — no new thread is created. The method behaves like any regular method call. Only start() creates a new OS thread and schedules the run() method to execute in that new thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the critical difference between invoking a method and creating a new thread of execution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling run() in test code and wondering why operations aren't happening concurrently or in parallel.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that start() is a native method that asks the JVM to allocate OS resources for a new thread and schedule run() on it.

sections.title: The Critical Difference Between run() and start()
sections.content:
This is one of the most important distinctions in Java concurrency. **Calling run() directly** is just a normal method call — it executes in the current thread, synchronously, like any other method. **Calling start()** is fundamentally different: it asks the JVM to create a new operating system thread, allocate resources for it, and schedule the run() method to execute in that new thread.

Think of it like the difference between reading a recipe yourself versus hiring a chef to cook it in a separate kitchen. The start() method is **native** — it's implemented in C/C++ and talks directly to the operating system to create an actual OS-level thread. After calling start(), the original thread and the new thread run in parallel, potentially on different CPU cores. The new thread has its own call stack, program counter, and local variables.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|start()|~Spawns a new thread|JVM then calls run()|runs concurrently|once per Thread
blue|run()|~Plain method call|same thread|no concurrency|like any method
emerald|The Trap|~Calling run() directly|no new thread|sequential execution|a silent bug
violet|IllegalThreadState|~start() twice|cannot restart|one thread, one start|create a new instance

sections.title: Demonstrating run() vs start() Behavior
When This Matters in Production
sections.content: This distinction is critical in **REST API services** handling concurrent requests. If you call run() instead of start() when spawning background tasks, each request blocks until its task completes, destroying your service's throughput. In a Spring Boot controller that sends emails asynchronously, calling run() would make every API request wait for email sending to finish — defeating the purpose. You'd see 100% CPU on one core while other cores sit idle. **Always use start()** when you need concurrent execution. The only time you'd call run() directly is in unit tests where you want to execute the task synchronously in the test thread to verify logic without dealing with thread timing issues. In production code for a service that processes orders concurrently, start() is mandatory.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling run() in request handlers**: Freshers write code like new Thread(task).run() in a REST controller, thinking they've made it asynchronous, but it blocks the request thread completely. The code compiles and runs but handles one request at a time.
- **Not observing interleaved output**: When testing with start(), freshers expect sequential output and get confused when thread outputs interleave. They think the code is broken when it's actually working correctly.
- **Calling start() multiple times**: After calling start(), freshers try to reuse the thread by calling start() again, which throws IllegalThreadStateException. Each Thread object can only transition from NEW to RUNNABLE once in its lifecycle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **run() is a regular method**: Calling it directly executes in the current thread, no concurrency happens
- **start() creates a new thread**: It's a native method that asks the OS to allocate a new thread of execution
- **Thread states**: start() transitions thread from NEW to RUNNABLE, then JVM scheduler invokes run()
- **Parallel execution**: Only start() allows multiple tasks to execute simultaneously on different cores
- **Can only start() once**: Each Thread instance can only be started once, throws IllegalThreadStateException otherwise
- **run() for testing**: Directly calling run() is useful in unit tests to execute task logic synchronously
- **Thread naming**: Use Thread.currentThread().getName() in run() to see which thread is executing the code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: If you call run instead of start on a Thread, no new thread is created at all. The run method just executes as a normal method call in your current thread, completely synchronously. It's like calling any other method on an object. Only start creates an actual new thread of execution. The start method is a native method that talks to the operating system to allocate a new OS thread with its own call stack and program counter. After you call start, the JVM schedules the run method to execute in that new thread, and both threads run in parallel. This matters a lot in production. If you're building a REST service and you call run instead of start for background tasks, every request will block until the task finishes, killing your throughput. You'd be using only one CPU core while the others sit idle. A common mistake freshers make is writing new Thread task dot run thinking they've made it concurrent, but it just blocks. In unit tests, though, calling run directly is actually useful because you can test the task logic synchronously without dealing with thread timing. So always use start in production code when you need real concurrency.

questions.question: How do you create a thread using a lambda expression in Java 8?
questions.title: Creating Threads with Lambda Expressions
questions.direct_answer: Since Runnable is a functional interface, you can use a lambda expression directly as the Runnable argument to the Thread constructor. This is the most concise way to create a thread for short inline tasks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Runnable is a functional interface and awareness of modern Java syntax for concurrency.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that any functional interface can be replaced with a lambda, thinking lambdas are only for Stream API operations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show all three syntaxes side-by-side: anonymous class, lambda, and method reference — explain when each is clearest.

sections.title: Lambda Expressions for Thread Creation
sections.content:
Since Java 8, **Runnable is a functional interface** — it has exactly one abstract method (run), making it eligible for lambda syntax. Instead of creating a full class or anonymous inner class, you can pass a lambda directly to the Thread constructor.

Think of it like ordering food: the old way required filling out a form with all details, while lambdas let you just say what you want. The lambda syntax is **() -> { code }** where the empty parentheses represent run()'s no-argument signature and the curly braces contain the thread's work. This is especially clean for short background tasks like logging, sending notifications, or quick data transformations. The **@FunctionalInterface** annotation on Runnable signals the compiler that it's designed for lambda use. For really short one-liners, you can omit the curly braces entirely.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable Lambda|~Functional interface|() arrow body|no anon class|since Java 8
blue|Pass to Thread|~Concise creation|new Thread(lambda)|.start()|readable
emerald|Method Reference|~Even cleaner|obj::process|when signature fits|reuse methods
violet|Capture|~Effectively final|locals captured|no mutation|share via fields/atomics

sections.title: Three Syntaxes for Creating Threads
When to Use Each Syntax
sections.content:
Use **lambda expressions** for short inline tasks of 1-5 lines — like sending an event notification, updating a cache entry, or logging an audit trail. They're perfect in Spring controllers for quick background work: new Thread(() -> auditLogger.log(userId)).start().

Use **method references** when you're delegating to an existing method that matches Runnable's signature — it's the clearest syntax when the logic already exists elsewhere.

Use **anonymous classes** only when you need to share state across multiple methods or override additional methods beyond run(). For complex multi-step tasks, create a separate class implementing Runnable rather than cramming everything into a lambda — if the lambda body exceeds 10 lines, extract it to a proper class.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trying to pass parameters to the lambda**: Freshers write () -> processOrder(orderId) but don't understand where orderId comes from — forgetting that lambdas capture variables from the enclosing scope. The variable must be effectively final.
- **Using method references incorrectly**: Writing service::processOrder(123) instead of () -> service.processOrder(123) — method references can't pass arguments directly.
- **Not understanding capture semantics**: Modifying a captured local variable inside the lambda, which causes a compiler error because captured variables must be effectively final. The variable can be read but not reassigned.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Functional interface**: Runnable has exactly one abstract method, making it lambda-compatible since Java 8
- **Lambda syntax**: () -> { code } where empty parens match run()'s no-argument signature
- **Variable capture**: Lambdas can access effectively final variables from enclosing scope, useful for passing data
- **Method reference**: Use :: syntax when delegating to existing method that matches Runnable signature
- **Conciseness trade-off**: Lambdas are cleaner for short tasks but hurt readability for complex logic
- **No return value**: Runnable's run() returns void, so the lambda body can't return anything
- **Modern best practice**: Lambda threads for quick tasks, separate Runnable classes for complex business logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You can create a thread using a lambda expression because Runnable is a functional interface with exactly one abstract method. Just pass a lambda directly to the Thread constructor, like new Thread opening paren lambda closing paren. The lambda syntax is opening paren closing paren arrow opening brace your code closing brace. For example, new Thread opening paren opening paren closing paren arrow System dot out dot println opening paren quote Processing quote closing paren closing paren dot start. The empty parentheses match the run method's no-argument signature. If it's a one-liner, you can skip the curly braces. This is way more concise than the old anonymous inner class approach where you had to write new Runnable with the whole override block. You can also use method references if you're just delegating to an existing method — like new Thread opening paren service colon colon processOrder closing paren. The lambda can capture variables from the surrounding scope as long as they're effectively final, which means you can read them but not reassign them. Use lambdas for short inline tasks like logging or sending notifications. If the logic is complex or more than ten lines, extract it to a proper Runnable class instead of cramming it into a lambda, because readability matters more than brevity.

questions.question: What is Callable and how does it differ from Runnable?
questions.title: Callable vs Runnable in Java
questions.direct_answer: Callable is like Runnable but its call() method returns a value and can throw checked exceptions. It's used with ExecutorService.submit() which returns a Future — letting you retrieve the result later.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how to get results back from concurrent operations and handle exceptions in threads.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to retrieve the value from a Callable, or not understanding that Future.get() blocks until the result is ready.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Future.get() blocking behavior and mention timeout options like get(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) to avoid hanging forever.

sections.title: Callable: Threads That Return Results
sections.content:
**Callable** is Java's interface for tasks that produce a result, unlike Runnable which can't return anything.

The key difference is the **call() method** which returns a generic type T and can throw checked exceptions — making it suitable for operations like database queries, REST API calls, or file parsing where you need the result and must handle errors. Think of Runnable as a worker who just does the job, while Callable is a worker who brings back a report. You submit Callable tasks to an **ExecutorService** using submit(), which immediately returns a **Future<T>** object. The Future is like a claim ticket — you can check if the task is done with isDone(), wait for completion with get(), or cancel it with cancel(). This pattern is fundamental in production services that need to run multiple operations concurrently and collect their results.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable|~run() to void|no checked exc|execute()|no result
blue|Callable|~call() to T|throws checked exc|submit() to Future|returns a value
emerald|Future|~Holds the result|get() blocks|isDone()/cancel()|exceptions surfaced
violet|Pick|~Need result/exc?|yes - Callable|no - Runnable|both pool-friendly

sections.title: Callable vs Runnable
sections.content:
| Aspect | Runnable | Callable<T> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Method signature | void run() | T call() throws Exception |
| Return value | Cannot return result | Returns typed result |
| Exception handling | Must catch checked exceptions internally | Can throw checked exceptions to caller |
| Executor usage | submit() or execute() | submit() only, returns Future<T> |
| Use case | Fire and forget background tasks | Tasks requiring result or status |

sections.title: Callable with Future Result Retrieval
When to Use Callable vs Runnable
sections.content:
Use **Callable** when you need a result back from the concurrent operation: fetching user profiles from a database, calling external REST APIs to aggregate data, or performing calculations that produce a value. In a microservice that calculates shipping costs from three providers concurrently, each provider check is a Callable returning the cost.

Use **Runnable** for fire-and-forget tasks that produce side effects but no return value: sending email notifications, writing audit logs, updating caches, or triggering webhooks. If the task might throw a checked exception like IOException or SQLException that you want the caller to handle, Callable is the only choice. For tasks that need results in a Spring Boot controller, Callable with Future lets you start multiple operations, do other work, then collect results at the end.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not handling Future.get() blocking**: Freshers call future.get() immediately after submit, not realizing it blocks the current thread until the result is ready — losing all concurrency benefits. Call get() only after starting all tasks.
- **Ignoring ExecutionException**: When the Callable throws an exception, get() wraps it in ExecutionException. Freshers catch Exception generically and lose the actual cause — always call getCause() to unwrap the real error.
- **No timeout on get()**: Calling future.get() without a timeout can hang forever if the task is stuck. Use get with timeout parameter in production: future.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) to fail fast instead of hanging indefinitely.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **call() returns value**: Unlike run() which returns void, call() returns a typed result of type T
- **Checked exceptions allowed**: call() declares throws Exception, so you can throw IOException, SQLException without catching
- **Future<T> pattern**: submit() returns Future immediately, actual result retrieved later with get()
- **Future.get() blocks**: Calling get() suspends the current thread until the task completes, must plan carefully
- **Timeout protection**: Use get(timeout, TimeUnit) to avoid hanging forever if task is stuck or slow
- **ExecutionException wrapping**: Exceptions thrown in call() are wrapped in ExecutionException, unwrap with getCause()
- **Thread pool required**: Callable only works with ExecutorService, not with raw Thread objects

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Callable is like Runnable but designed for tasks that return a result. Instead of a run method that returns void, Callable has a call method that returns a typed value and can throw checked exceptions. You use it with ExecutorService by calling submit, which gives you back a Future object immediately. The Future is like a claim ticket — the task runs in the background, and you call future dot get to retrieve the result when you need it. The important thing to know is that get blocks the current thread until the result is ready, so you don't want to call it right after submit or you lose all concurrency. The pattern is submit all your tasks first, do other work, then call get on each Future at the end. In production, always use the timeout version of get — like future dot get five seconds TimeUnit dot SECONDS — so your code doesn't hang forever if a task gets stuck. If the Callable throws an exception, get wraps it in ExecutionException, so you need to call getCause to unwrap the actual error. Use Callable when you need results back from concurrent operations, like fetching data from multiple APIs or databases. Use Runnable for fire and forget tasks like logging or sending notifications.

questions.question: What is an ExecutorService and why is it preferred over creating threads directly?
questions.title: ExecutorService vs Raw Thread Creation
questions.direct_answer: ExecutorService manages a thread pool, reusing threads instead of creating and destroying them for each task. This avoids the overhead of OS thread creation, controls concurrency, and provides lifecycle management — making it the standard approach in production Java code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands production-grade thread management and the problems with creating raw Thread objects.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a new Thread for every incoming request in a web service, which causes resource exhaustion under load.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the Executors factory methods like newFixedThreadPool, explain bounded vs unbounded pools, and mention shutdown vs shutdownNow.

sections.title: Thread Pools and Production Thread Management
sections.content:
**ExecutorService** is Java's high-level API for managing a pool of worker threads that execute tasks submitted to them. Instead of creating a new operating system thread for each task (which is expensive and slow), a thread pool maintains a fixed or dynamic set of threads that pick up tasks from a queue and execute them.

Think of it like a restaurant kitchen: instead of hiring a new chef every time an order comes in, you have a team of chefs who continuously process orders from a queue. Creating an OS thread involves system calls, memory allocation for the thread's stack (typically 1MB), and scheduler registration — costing thousands of CPU cycles. **Thread pools** eliminate this overhead by reusing threads across tasks. ExecutorService also provides **lifecycle management** (shutdown, task cancellation), **bounded concurrency** (control max threads), and **task queuing** (handle bursts). This is the standard approach in production Java services.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Raw Thread|~new Thread().start()|created per task|no reuse|unbounded = risky
blue|ExecutorService|~Managed pool|reuses threads|bounded queue|shutdown lifecycle
emerald|Why Pool|~Cost control|no per-task creation|backpressure|tunable size
violet|Common APIs|~Factory methods|newFixedThreadPool|newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor|submit/invokeAll

sections.title: Using ExecutorService Instead of Raw Threads
When to Use ExecutorService
sections.content:
Use **ExecutorService** in any production service handling concurrent operations: REST APIs processing multiple requests, batch jobs processing files in parallel, microservices making concurrent database queries or external API calls. For a Spring Boot application, Spring's **@Async** annotation uses a thread pool under the hood, but if you're managing threads directly, always use ExecutorService.

Use **newFixedThreadPool(n)** when you know the concurrency level (like number of CPU cores for CPU-bound tasks, or I/O operations with known limits).

Use **newCachedThreadPool()** for short-lived tasks with unpredictable load, but beware it can create unbounded threads under heavy load.

Use **newScheduledThreadPool(n)** for recurring tasks like health checks every 30 seconds. Never create raw Thread objects in request handlers — each HTTP request in a service handling 1000 requests/second would create 1000 OS threads, exhausting system resources.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Creating unbounded threads**: Freshers write new Thread(...).start() in a loop, creating thousands of threads for a batch job with 10,000 items. The JVM runs out of memory or the OS hits thread limits. Each thread consumes 1MB stack space, so 10,000 threads = 10GB RAM just for stacks.
- **Not shutting down the executor**: After finishing tasks, freshers forget to call executor.shutdown(), leaving threads alive and preventing JVM exit. The application hangs at shutdown because non-daemon threads are still running.
- **Using execute() instead of submit()**: The execute method doesn't return a Future, so you can't check task status or get exceptions. If a task throws an exception, it's silently lost unless you add a try-catch inside the task.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Thread pool reuse**: Threads are created once and reused for multiple tasks, avoiding OS thread creation overhead
- **Bounded concurrency**: Fixed pool size prevents resource exhaustion, controls max parallel operations
- **Task queue**: When all threads are busy, new tasks wait in a queue until a thread becomes available
- **Executors factory methods**: newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newScheduledThreadPool create different pool types
- **shutdown() vs shutdownNow()**: shutdown waits for tasks to complete, shutdownNow interrupts running tasks immediately
- **awaitTermination()**: Blocks until all tasks complete or timeout expires, used in graceful shutdown
- **submit() returns Future**: Unlike execute(), submit returns Future to track task status and retrieve results

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: ExecutorService is Java's thread pool API that manages a set of worker threads for you instead of creating new threads for every task. Creating an OS thread is expensive — it takes thousands of CPU cycles and allocates about one megabyte for the thread's stack. If you're handling a thousand requests per second and create a new thread for each one, you'd create a thousand threads per second, which quickly exhausts memory and CPU. A thread pool solves this by creating threads once and reusing them. You submit tasks to the pool, and available threads pick them up from a queue. This is the standard approach in production. You create an ExecutorService using factory methods like Executors dot newFixedThreadPool opening paren ten closing paren for a pool of ten threads. Then you submit tasks with executor dot submit opening paren lambda closing paren. The huge advantage is bounded concurrency — you control exactly how many operations run in parallel, preventing resource exhaustion under load. Always call shutdown when you're done to release the threads, and use awaitTermination to wait for tasks to complete gracefully. A common mistake freshers make is creating a new Thread in a loop for batch processing, which creates thousands of threads and crashes the application. Another mistake is forgetting to shut down the executor, so threads stay alive and block JVM exit.

questions.question: What is a daemon thread in Java and when would you use one?
questions.title: Daemon Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: A daemon thread is a background thread that is automatically killed when all non-daemon (user) threads finish. Set with thread.setDaemon(true) before start(). Use for background services like logging, cleanup, or monitoring that should not prevent JVM shutdown.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM lifecycle and how threads affect application shutdown behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting daemon status after calling start(), which throws IllegalThreadStateException and has no effect.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete production example like a health check monitor that polls metrics every 5 seconds but shouldn't block application shutdown.

sections.title: Daemon Threads and JVM Shutdown Behavior
sections.content:
A **daemon thread** is a background service thread that the JVM automatically terminates when all user (non-daemon) threads complete.

The key distinction is that the JVM keeps running as long as at least one non-daemon thread is alive, but **daemon threads don't prevent JVM shutdown**. Think of daemon threads like background music at a party — when all guests leave, the music stops automatically. You mark a thread as daemon by calling **setDaemon(true)** before calling start(). The default is false (non-daemon/user thread). Java's garbage collector, finalizer, and signal handlers run as daemon threads.

In production, you use daemon threads for tasks like periodic health checks, log file cleanup, or cache refresh that should run while the application is active but shouldn't block shutdown. The JVM shutdown sequence is: all non-daemon threads finish → JVM calls shutdown hooks → JVM terminates all daemon threads abruptly → JVM exits.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Daemon Thread|~Background helper|setDaemon(true)|before start()|dies with the JVM
blue|User Thread|~Default|keeps the JVM alive|JVM waits for it|non-daemon
emerald|JVM Exit|~When daemons die|all user threads done|daemons killed abruptly|no finally guarantee
violet|Use For|~Support tasks|monitoring, cleanup|cache eviction|never critical work

sections.title: Creating and Using Daemon Threads
When to Use Daemon Threads
sections.content:
Use **daemon threads** for background services that support the main application but aren't critical: periodic health checks polling service status every few seconds, cache cleanup tasks removing stale entries every hour, log file rotation checking size limits, or metrics collectors sending data to monitoring systems. In a Spring Boot REST API, you might have a daemon thread monitoring request queue depth and logging warnings.

Use **non-daemon (user) threads** for critical business operations that must complete: processing customer orders, writing data to the database, sending confirmation emails, or completing transactions. If a payment processing thread were daemon and the JVM started shutting down, the payment might be interrupted mid-transaction. The rule: daemon threads for nice-to-have monitoring, non-daemon for must-complete business logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting daemon after start()**: Freshers call thread.setDaemon(true) after thread.start(), which throws IllegalThreadStateException because the thread's daemon status can only be set before it starts running. The call silently has no effect if caught.
- **Using daemon for critical work**: Setting a thread as daemon when it performs important operations like writing to a database or sending API responses. When the JVM shuts down, the thread is killed mid-operation, potentially causing data corruption or incomplete transactions.
- **Expecting graceful shutdown**: Daemon threads are terminated abruptly by the JVM without any cleanup or finally blocks executing. Freshers expect catch or finally to run, but the thread just dies instantly when all non-daemon threads exit.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Daemon definition**: Background thread that doesn't prevent JVM shutdown, killed automatically when all user threads exit
- **setDaemon(true)**: Must be called before start(), throws IllegalThreadStateException if called after
- **JVM shutdown rule**: JVM exits when all non-daemon threads complete, regardless of running daemon threads
- **Abrupt termination**: Daemon threads are killed without cleanup, finally blocks don't execute
- **Default status**: Threads are non-daemon by default, inherit parent thread's daemon status if created by another thread
- **Built-in daemons**: Garbage collector, finalizer, and reference handler are JVM daemon threads
- **Production use cases**: Health checks, cache cleanup, log rotation, metrics collection — non-critical background tasks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A daemon thread is a background service thread that doesn't prevent the JVM from shutting down. The JVM keeps running as long as there's at least one non-daemon thread alive, but daemon threads don't count toward that. When all non-daemon threads finish, the JVM immediately kills all daemon threads and exits, even if those daemon threads are in the middle of work. You make a thread daemon by calling setDaemon opening paren true closing paren before calling start — if you call it after start, it throws IllegalThreadStateException. Use daemon threads for background monitoring tasks that support the application but aren't critical, like a health check that polls service status every five seconds or a cleanup task that removes stale cache entries. For example, in a REST API, you might have a daemon thread logging queue depth every ten seconds. That's useful while the app runs, but you don't want it to block shutdown when you stop the service. The key thing is daemon threads are killed abruptly without cleanup — no finally blocks execute. So never use daemon threads for critical operations like database writes or sending API responses. A common mistake is setting a thread as daemon when it does important work, then being surprised when data is lost during shutdown. Always use non-daemon threads for business logic that must complete.
